questions.text: What triggers a push and a pull ('the usual triggers')? Which ones, and does a push always come before a pull?
questions.about: Sync is push plus pull, on the usual triggers

questions.text: What exactly does Phone A send in a Push? Is it each outbox entry as a change with its own change ID, and what does the server's 'Result' contain?
questions.about: A->>S: Push / S-->>A: Result

questions.text: What is the version check? Where does each phone's note version come from, and what does the server compare when B pushes?
questions.about: Conflicts are handled by version check

questions.text: When B gets 'Conflict', what happens on the phone: is the conflict copy created by the server or by Phone B, what does it contain, and who sees which version as the original?
questions.about: S-->>B: Conflict / conflict copy

questions.text: What are the 'processed change IDs' and how are they used on a retry? What does the server reply when it sees a change ID it already processed?
questions.about: Retries use change IDs

questions.text: What does 'Sent changes aren't edited' mean for a note the user keeps editing while a push is in flight or before its result arrives?
questions.about: Sent changes aren't edited

questions.text: What is the cursor, who stores it (phone or server), and what is it a position in? How does the change log feed the paged pull, and when does the phone advance the cursor?
questions.about: A cursor tracks pull progress, paged

questions.text: What are the batching limits, on push and on pull, and what happens when the outbox or the changes exceed them? What happens if a push or pull fails or times out midway?
questions.about: Batching limits apply

answers.text: Three triggers: connection returns, app comes to the foreground, and every 60 seconds while online. Each sync always pushes first, then pulls. Added to the notes.

Each outbox entry is one change with its own change ID, note ID, full body and starting version, up to 100 per push. Result per change is accepted plus new version, or conflict plus the conflict note ID. Added.
Each phone's starting version is the server version its note had when last pulled or accepted. The server compares it with the note's current version; equal is accepted, otherwise conflict. Added.

The server creates the conflict note from B's body, titled with the original title plus ' (conflict)', and logs it. B removes the change from its outbox and its next pull brings the winning version of the original (A's) and the conflict note. Added.
The server remembers each processed change ID with its result. On a retry of a known ID it replies with the stored result and applies nothing. Added.

Once a change is in a push it is frozen, so a retry sends identical content. Edits made meanwhile become a new queued change, whose starting version is updated to the new version from the result. Added.

The cursor is a sequence number in the server change log, stored on the phone: the highest entry applied. The pull returns entries after it, max 500, with next cursor. The phone advances it in the same local transaction that applies the page. Added.

Push batch max 100 changes, pull page max 500 entries; extra work goes in further batches or pages in the same sync. If a push or pull fails midway, the outbox and cursor are unchanged, so the next sync repeats it safely thanks to change IDs and idempotent applying. Added.

questions.text: After A's push is accepted, the sequence shows A pulling. What does A's pull return for A's own edit, and does A just ignore it because the version is not newer?
questions.about: A->>S: Pull (after cursor) / Log entries, next cursor

questions.text: When B's push gets a conflict, B's outbox change is removed and B's local note still has B's edited text. Between the result and B's pull, what does B see? And what if B's pull fails: is B's text lost from the UI?
questions.about: Conflict copy / B's local note is replaced by the winning version when B pulls

questions.text: The conflict note is a new note. Which note ID and starting version does it get, and is it just a normal note that can be edited and synced afterwards?
questions.about: Conflict copy: the server saves the losing body as a new note

questions.text: A new note created on a phone has no server version yet. What starting version does its first push carry, and how does the server decide it is accepted?
questions.about: Push: starting version (the server version the edit began from)

questions.text: When an edit is queued while a change is in flight and the result is a conflict, what version does the new queued change get as its starting version? Does it then conflict too?
questions.about: Changes in flight: the new change's starting version becomes the version from the result

questions.text: If the server accepted a change but the response is lost, and the user edited the note meanwhile, how does the retry stay safe? Does the retry return the stored result, and what happens to the newer queued change?
questions.about: Retries: the server returns the stored result and applies nothing twice

questions.text: What if the first change in a push batch fails on the server (error, not conflict)? Are the other changes in that batch still processed, and which are removed from the outbox?
questions.about: Push: up to 100 outbox changes, oldest first / Result per change

answers.text: A's pull does return A's own entry. A ignores it because on an accepted result A already set its local version to the new version, so the entry is not newer. Added to Result.

Between the result and the pull, B keeps seeing its own text. It is also stored on the server in the conflict note. If the pull fails, the UI is unchanged and the next sync repeats the pull, so nothing is lost. Added to Conflict copy.
The server gives the conflict note a new note ID and version 1. It is an ordinary note that can be edited and synced. Added to Conflict copy.
A new note's first change carries starting version 0. The server treats an unknown note ID as current version 0, so it is accepted and becomes version 1. Added as New notes.

On an accepted result the new change takes the new version. On a conflict result it keeps its old starting version and will conflict too, producing another conflict note. I chose this because taking the current version would silently overwrite the winner's text. Clarified in Changes in flight and noted in open questions.

The retry sends the same frozen change and the server returns the stored result, applying nothing. The phone then sets the newer queued change's starting version from that accepted result, and sends it in a later batch, since the next batch waits for the previous results. Added to Retries and Push.

The server handles the batch in order and stops at the first unexpected error. It returns results only for changes already handled, and the phone removes only those. The rest stay in the outbox and are retried next sync, which is safe because of change IDs. If a change always errors, it blocks the ones behind it. I have no decided limit for that, so it is listed as an open question.

questions.text: The diagram shows B's push getting a conflict after A's was accepted. What exactly tells the server B's edit lost: B's starting version (say 3) vs the note's current version (4 after A)? And what do A and B each hold as the note's version before any pull?
questions.about: Version check: the server compares the starting version with the note's current version

questions.text: If B's pull after a conflict returns A's edit, how does B's phone decide to replace its local text? Is it only because the entry's version is newer than B's local version, and what version does B's local note have at that moment?
questions.about: Conflict copy: B's local note is replaced by the winning version

questions.text: When a note changes through a pull, what happens if the user has a queued, unsent edit on that same note at that moment? Is the local text overwritten and the outbox change kept?
questions.about: Edits: every edit is saved to local SQLite at once and also queued in the outbox

questions.text: Collapsing several edits into one change keeps the original starting version. What if the earlier change is already in flight (frozen)? Does collapsing stop and a new change start, and does the new change get its own change ID?
questions.about: Several edits to one note before upload collapse into one queued change

questions.text: The change log entries: what does one contain (note ID, full body, version, title)? Does the conflict note appear as an ordinary entry with its own sequence number, and how does the phone create it locally from that entry?
questions.about: Log entries, next cursor

questions.text: When a push gets no response at all and the sync is abandoned, is the pull still done in that sync? And what does the 60 second timer do if a sync is still running when the next one is due?
questions.about: Triggers: every 60 seconds while online

questions.text: How does a phone that has never synced, or a new phone, get the existing notes? Does it pull from cursor 0 and receive every log entry from the start?
questions.about: Cursor: the phone stores the highest log sequence number it has applied

answers.text: Yes. Both phones hold the version they last got from the server, say 3. After A's accepted push the server is at 4. B's push carries starting version 3, which is not equal to 4, so it loses. Added as the Versions line with this example.
Yes. B's local note is still at version 3. The entry from A has version 4, which is newer, so the phone replaces its local title, body and version. Added as Applying an entry.

The pull replaces the local text and the queued change stays in the outbox. It keeps its old starting version, so it will conflict, and the server saves its body as a conflict note. Nothing is lost. I chose this over a special merge or skip rule because the brief rules out merging and the existing conflict path already preserves the text. Added to Applying an entry.

Collapsing only applies to a change that has not been sent. Once a change is in flight it is frozen, so the next edit starts a new queued change with its own new change ID. Added to Edits and Changes in flight.

An entry holds sequence number, note ID, title, full body and the note's version after the write. The conflict note is an ordinary entry with its own sequence number. The phone creates the note locally when it does not know the note ID. Added as Log entries and Applying an entry.

If a push gets no response, the sync is abandoned and the pull is not done; the next sync starts with a push again. If a sync is still running when the 60 second timer fires, that tick is skipped, which avoids two syncs sending the same changes at once. Added to Triggers and Server errors.
Yes. A new phone starts with cursor 0 and pulls every log entry from the beginning, 500 per page. This needs no extra mechanism. The log growing without limit is listed as an open question.

teachbacks.text:
1. Edit on the phone. The user edits a note. The phone writes it to its local SQLite straight away and shows it in the UI without waiting for the network. The same edit is queued in the outbox as a "change". A change holds a change ID, the note ID, the full body and a starting version. The starting version is the server version the phone last got for that note, from a pull or from an accepted result. A note created on the phone has no server version, so its change starts at version 0. If the user edits the same note again before upload, the unsent change is collapsed. It keeps the original starting version and takes the latest full body. A change that has already been sent is never collapsed into.

2. Sync trigger. A sync starts when the connection returns, when the app comes to the foreground, and every 60 seconds while online. If a sync is still running when the timer fires, that tick is skipped. A sync always pushes first, then pulls.

3. Push. The phone sends up to 100 outbox changes, oldest first. It handles the results of one batch before sending the next. It repeats until the outbox is empty, then moves to the pull. The changes in a push are now "frozen". A new edit to the same note becomes a separate queued change with a new change ID.

4. Server version check. For each change, the server compares the change's starting version with the note's current version on the server. An unknown note ID counts as version 0.
   - Equal: accepted. The note's version goes up by 1, and an entry is appended to the change log. The entry has the next sequence number, note ID, title, full body and the new version. This is how a brand-new note becomes version 1.
   - Not equal: conflict. The first write to reach the server wins. The server saves the losing body as a new conflict note. It has a new note ID, version 1, and the title "<original title> (conflict)". It is logged as an ordinary entry.
   - In both cases the server stores the result under the change ID. If the same change ID arrives again, it returns the stored result and applies nothing.

5. Phone handles the results. For each change, the server returns either accepted with the new version, or conflict with the conflict note ID. On either result the phone removes the change from the outbox.
   - Accepted: the phone sets its local note's version to the new version. When its own edit comes back in the pull, it is not newer than the local copy and is ignored. A newer edit queued during the push gets its starting version set to this new version.
   - Conflict: the phone keeps showing its own text until it pulls. That text is safe in the conflict note. An edit queued during the push keeps its old starting version, so it will conflict too. The document accepts this.

6. Pull. After the outbox is empty, the phone asks for log entries after its cursor, at most 500 at a time. The server replies with the entries, the next cursor, and whether more remain. The phone keeps asking until nothing remains. For each page it applies the entries and saves the new cursor in one local transaction. A new phone starts at cursor 0 and receives the whole log.

7. Apply an entry. If the phone does not know the note ID, it creates the note. If it does know it, it replaces the local title, body and version only when the entry's version is newer than its local version.
   - In the example, B's version-3 note is replaced by A's version-4 text.
   - The conflict note arrives in the same pull as a new note.
   - If the user has an unsent change queued for that note, the local text is still replaced. The queued change stays in the outbox with its old starting version. It will conflict later, and its body will then be saved as a conflict note.

8. Failures, where the document says.
   - Push gets no response: nothing is removed from the outbox, and the sync is abandoned without pulling. The next sync resends the same frozen change. The change ID makes the repeat safe, even if the user edited the note in the meantime.
   - Server hits an unexpected error in a batch: the server handles changes in order and stops. It returns results only for the changes already handled. The phone removes only those and keeps the rest.
   - Pull drops midway: the cursor moves only after a page is applied, so the next sync repeats the same request. The UI is unchanged until a pull succeeds.
   - An entry applied twice: harmless, because an entry that is not newer than the local version is ignored.
   - Open issues: a change that fails with a server error every time blocks the changes behind it, and no retry or skip rule exists. The log is never trimmed, so a new phone's first pull grows over time.
gaps: How the phone tells that a push got no response (timeout length, what counts as a failure) is not stated. The document also does not say whether the sync retries at once or only waits for the next trigger.

How the server deals with a repeated change ID is not fully described. The server stores each result under the change ID. It is not stated whether that applies when the retry arrives in a different batch or after a later write to the same note.

Which title the phone sends and the server stores for an ordinary accepted change is not stated. A change is defined as note ID, full body and starting version, with no title field, yet each log entry has a title. Where the title comes from on an edit is unclear.
The collapse rule in step 1 says several edits collapse into one change, but not which change ID the collapsed change keeps.

What happens to the unsent queued change when a pull replaces the local text is only partly explained. The document does not say how the phone tracks that the local text and the queued body now differ, or what the user sees until the conflict note arrives.

The server's response to the phone's push or pull is not described when the server reports an unexpected error mid-batch. The document does not say what the phone does with the unprocessed rest, such as whether it still pulls in that sync.
teachbacks.notes: The change was defined without a title, yet the server logs a title for each accepted write and titles conflict notes from the original title. The document never said where the title comes from. A change must carry the note's title.; The collapse rule did not say which change ID a collapsed change keeps. It keeps the ID of the unsent change it collapses into.; A server error mid-batch did not say what the phone does with the unprocessed rest, or whether it still pulls in that sync. It removes the handled changes, keeps the rest, and abandons the sync without pulling, as for no response.

teachbacks.text:
Walkthrough: Phone B edits note N (server version 3) offline while Phone A also edits N offline. Both start from version 3.

1. Edit on the phone. B edits N. The edit is saved to local SQLite at once and shown in the UI, with no network wait. The edit is also queued in the outbox as a change. The change holds a change ID, note ID, the note's current title, the full body (no diffs) and a starting version. Here the starting version is 3, the version B last got from the server. If B edits N again before the change is sent, the edits collapse into one change. That change keeps its change ID and original starting version and takes the latest title and body. A note created on the phone has no server version, so its first change carries starting version 0. The local SQLite database and the outbox are the phone's state.

2. What starts a sync. A sync starts when the connection returns, when the app comes to the foreground, and every 60 seconds while online. If a sync is still running when the timer fires, that tick is skipped. Every sync pushes first, then pulls.

3. Push. The phone sends up to 100 outbox changes, oldest first. Each carries change ID, note ID, title, full body and starting version. It sends the next batch only after handling the results of the previous one. It repeats until the outbox is empty, then pulls. Once a change is part of a push it is frozen, so it can no longer be collapsed into.

4. Version check on the server. For each change, the server compares the change's starting version with the note's current version. An unknown note ID counts as version 0, so a new note is accepted and becomes version 1.
   - If they are equal, the change is accepted. The note's version goes up by one. An entry is appended to the change log with the next sequence number, the change's title and body, and the note's new version.
   - If they are not equal, it is a conflict. The first write to reach the server wins. In the example, A's push arrives first and is accepted, and the note goes to version 4. B's change carries starting version 3, which is not 4, so it is a conflict. The server saves B's body as a new conflict note. The conflict note has a new note ID, version 1 and the title "<original title> (conflict)". It is logged as an ordinary entry. No text is merged and none is lost.
   - Either way, the server stores the result under the change ID. If it sees that ID again, in any batch or later, it returns the stored result and applies nothing. The server's state here is the notes with their versions, the change log, and the processed change IDs with their results.

5. The phone handles the results. For each change the server returns either accepted with the new version, or conflict with the conflict note ID. The phone removes the change from the outbox on either result.
   - On accepted, the phone also sets the local note's version to the new version. When that edit later comes back in a pull, it is not newer than the local copy and is ignored.
   - If the user edits the note while its change is in flight, that makes a new queued change with a new change ID. If the earlier result was accepted, the new change's starting version becomes the new version. If it was a conflict, the new change keeps the old starting version and will conflict too. The document accepts this.
   - After a conflict, B keeps seeing its own text until it pulls. That text is safe in the conflict note on the server.

6. Pull. After the push loop finishes, the phone asks the server for log entries after its cursor, at most 500. The cursor is the highest sequence number the phone has applied, and the phone stores it. The server replies with the entries, the next cursor and whether more remain. The phone keeps pulling until none remain. It applies each page and saves the new cursor together in one local transaction. A new phone starts at cursor 0 and receives every entry, 500 at a time.

7. Apply each entry on the phone. If the phone does not know the note ID, it creates the note. If it does, it replaces the local title, body and version only when the entry's version is newer than the local version. In the example, B pulls and gets A's version 4 entry. That replaces B's local version 3 text. B also gets the conflict-note entry, which creates a new note holding B's lost text. If the user has an unsent change queued for that note, the local text is still replaced. The queued change stays in the outbox with its old starting version. It will conflict later, and its body will be saved as a conflict note.

8. Failure handling. A failure is any push or pull that does not return a normal response. The phone does not retry at once. The next trigger starts the next sync.
   - If a push gets no response, nothing is removed from the outbox, and the sync is abandoned without pulling. The next sync pushes the same frozen changes again. The stored results by change ID make the repeat safe, even if the user edited the note meanwhile.
   - If the server hits an unexpected error (not a conflict) in a batch, it handles the batch in order and stops. It returns results only for the changes already handled. The phone removes only those, keeps the rest, and abandons the sync without pulling. The next sync pushes the rest.
   - If a pull drops midway, the cursor only moves after a page is applied, so the next sync repeats the same request. The UI is unchanged until a pull succeeds.
   - If an entry is applied twice, it is harmless, because the phone ignores an entry whose version is not newer than its local copy.

9. Known limits the document accepts. An edit made after a conflict but before a pull will conflict again. A change that fails with a server error every time blocks the changes behind it, and no retry limit or skip rule is decided. The change log is never trimmed, so a new phone's first pull grows with the log.
gaps: The document does not say how the phone and server agree on the next change log sequence number or version when two pushes arrive at the same moment, so how 'first to reach the server wins' is enforced is unexplained.
It does not say how the phone's cursor in a pull request is sent or what the 'next cursor' value is when no entries remain (for example whether it equals the old cursor).
It does not say how the phone's push results are matched to the changes in a batch, or what happens to the rest of the batch after a server error beyond 'stops'.
It does not say what happens on the phone when a conflict result arrives for a change whose note has since been edited again, apart from the new change conflicting later.
It does not say what the phone does to the local note's version after a conflict result. The note stays at the old version until a pull, but this is not stated explicitly.
